title: Composition versus inheritance
summary: Is-a, has-a, and why "favour composition" is common advice.

recallPrompts.prompt: What is the difference between composition and inheritance? Give an example of each.
Why do people say "favour composition over inheritance"?
When is inheritance still the right choice?

mentalModel.analogy: Inheritance is **family resemblance**: you get your parents' traits whether you want them or not, and you can't swap them later. Composition is **assembling a team**: you pick the specialists you need, and you can replace one without rebuilding everyone else.

sections.heading: Is-a versus has-a
sections.body:
**Inheritance** models **is-a**: a `Dog` is an `Animal`. **Composition** models **has-a**: a `Car` has an `Engine`, so it holds one in a field and **delegates** work to it (`car.start()` calls `engine.start()`).

A quick test is to say the sentence. "A car is an engine" is nonsense, so a car must *have* one. If both sentences sound odd, the classes probably shouldn't be linked at all.

sections.heading: What goes wrong with deep inheritance
sections.body:
Inheritance is the tightest coupling in OOP. The child depends on the parent's internals, not just its public interface.

- **Fragile base class**: a harmless-looking change to a parent can break subclasses you didn't know about.
- **Rigid hierarchies**: a `Duck` class with `fly()` works until you need a rubber duck that can't fly, then a robot duck that flies with rockets. You end up overriding methods to do nothing, or with combinations like `FlyingQuackingDuck`.
- **Fixed at compile time**: an object can't change its parent while running.
- **Single parent**: Java, Kotlin and TypeScript allow only one superclass, so behaviours can't be mixed in from two.

sections.heading: Composition: build from parts
sections.body:
With composition, a class holds **objects that provide behaviour** and delegates to them:

- Behaviours combine freely: a duck gets *some* flying behaviour and *some* quacking behaviour.
- They can be **swapped at run time**, for example when a duck's wing is injured.
- Each part can be tested on its own, and a part's internals can change without touching the class that uses it.

This is the heart of the **strategy** pattern, and it fits with dependency injection from SOLID. Kotlin even has built-in delegation (`class Logger(w: Writer) : Writer by w`) to make it cheap.

sections.heading: When inheritance is right
Multiple inheritance and the diamond
sections.body:
If `C` inherits from both `A` and `B`, and both override a method from a shared parent, which version does `C` get? That is the **diamond problem**.

- **Java, Kotlin and TypeScript** avoid it: one superclass, but any number of **interfaces**.
- **Python** allows multiple inheritance and picks a method using a fixed **method resolution order** (MRO), which you can inspect with `C.__mro__`.

Mixing in behaviour through composition, or through interfaces with default methods, sidesteps the problem entirely.

explainBack.prompt: Explain composition and inheritance, why "favour composition" is common advice, and when you would still choose inheritance.

rubric.point: Inheritance models is-a; composition models has-a, holding parts and delegating to them.
Inheritance couples a child to its parent's internals (fragile base class).
Hierarchies get rigid: behaviours can't be mixed or changed at run time.
Composition lets behaviours combine, be swapped at run time, and be tested alone.
Inheritance still fits true, stable is-a relationships and framework base classes.
Single-parent languages use interfaces; Python resolves multiple inheritance with the MRO.

checks.prompt: What is the "fragile base class" problem?
options: Base classes use too much memory.
A change inside a parent class can silently break subclasses that relied on how it worked internally.
Base classes can't have constructors.
Abstract classes can't be instantiated.
checks.explanation: Subclasses often depend on a parent's internal behaviour, not just its public interface, so the parent can't change safely.

hints.text: How tightly is a subclass tied to its parent?

checks.prompt: A game character's attack style must change mid-game, from sword to bow. Which design handles that best?
options: SwordCharacter and BowCharacter subclasses
A Character holding an AttackBehaviour field that can be replaced
A long if/else on a string

checks.explanation: Composition lets you swap the behaviour object at run time. An object can't change its class once it exists.

hints.text: Can an object change its class after it is created?

checks.prompt: `RubberDuck extends Duck` overrides `fly()` to do nothing. What does that suggest?
options: Good reuse of Duck's code.
The hierarchy is wrong: flying isn't a behaviour every duck shares, so it should be composed in.
RubberDuck should be abstract.
fly() should be private.
checks.explanation: Overriding to do nothing means the subclass can't honour the parent's promise. That is a Liskov smell. Model flying as a swappable behaviour instead.

hints.text: Can every Duck in this design actually fly?

checks.prompt: What does "favour composition over inheritance" mean?
options: Never use inheritance.
Default to composing behaviour from parts; use inheritance for genuine, stable is-a relationships.
Composition is faster at run time.
Inheritance is deprecated in modern languages.
checks.explanation: It is a default, not a ban. Inheritance stays right for true is-a types and framework base classes.

checks.prompt: In Android, your screen class extends `AppCompatActivity`. Is that a misuse of inheritance?
options: Yes: always use composition.
No: framework base classes are designed to be extended, and your screen genuinely is an activity.
Yes: Kotlin doesn't allow it.
Only if the class has more than ten methods.
checks.explanation: Frameworks often provide base classes built for subclassing. The problems come from deep hierarchies you invent yourself, not from extending one designed base class.

hints.text: Was that base class designed to be extended?

checks.prompt: How do Java and Kotlin avoid the diamond problem?
options: They pick a random parent's method.
A class can extend only one class, but implement many interfaces.
They ban interfaces.
They copy both methods.
checks.explanation: Single class inheritance avoids ambiguous implementations. If two interfaces provide clashing default methods, you must override the method and choose explicitly.

hints.text: How many superclasses can a Java or Kotlin class have?

checks.prompt: Python allows multiple inheritance. What is the name (or abbreviation) for the fixed order it uses to decide which parent's method runs?
checks.explanation: The **method resolution order (MRO)**, which you can inspect with `ClassName.__mro__`. It is computed with C3 linearisation.

hints.text: Three letters: the order Python resolves methods in.

options: The class forwards a call to an object it holds, which does the actual work.
The class inherits all of a parent's methods.
Methods are made private.
A subclass replaces a parent's method.
checks.explanation: `car.start()` calls `this.engine.start()`. The outer class presents the method and the part implements it.

hints.text: Who actually does the work when you call car.start()?

checks.prompt: Why is composition usually easier to unit test than a deep inheritance hierarchy?
options: Composed parts can be replaced with simple fakes, and each part can be tested on its own.
Composition runs faster in tests.
Test frameworks only support composition.
It isn't easier to test.
checks.explanation: Injected parts can be swapped for fakes, and each behaviour is a small class with its own tests. A deep hierarchy drags every ancestor into every test.

handsOn.prompt:
Build ducks with composition.

- `Wings` has `fly()` returning `"flies with wings"`. `CannotFly` has `fly()` returning `"can't fly"`.
- `Duck(name, flyer)` has `fly()`, returning the name, a space, then the flyer's text, e.g. `"Mallard flies with wings"`.
- `setFlyer(newFlyer)` swaps the behaviour at run time. (Python: `set_flyer`.)

Why is this better than `RubberDuck extends Duck` overriding `fly()`?

hints.text: Duck should not know how flying works. It should ask something else.
Composition with delegation: the strategy pattern.
Store the flyer in a field. fly() returns `${name} ${flyer.fly()}`. setFlyer replaces the field.

handsOn.explanation: The duck **has** a flying behaviour and **delegates** to it. A rubber duck is just `Duck('Rubber duck', CannotFly())`: no subclass that overrides `fly()` to do nothing, so there is no Liskov violation. Behaviours combine freely (add a quack behaviour the same way), can change at run time (an injured duck), and each one can be tested alone.
selfCheck: Duck contains no flying logic of its own; it delegates.
Swapping the flyer changes what fly() returns, without a new class.
I explained why the subclass-that-overrides-to-nothing approach is worse.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using inheritance just to reuse a few methods.
commonMistakes.fix: If it isn't a genuine is-a, hold the helper as a field and delegate to it.
The advice is "favour composition". Inheritance is right for true is-a types and designed framework base classes.

commonMistakes.mistake: Overriding a parent's method to do nothing or throw.
commonMistakes.fix: That breaks Liskov. Move the varying behaviour into a composed part.

commonMistakes.mistake: Building deep hierarchies to combine features (FlyingQuackingDuck…).
commonMistakes.fix: Combinations of behaviours are exactly what composition handles well.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting that an object can't change its class.
commonMistakes.fix: Behaviour that changes at run time must be composed in.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking multiple inheritance is free in Python.
commonMistakes.fix: It works, but method lookup follows the MRO. Keep hierarchies shallow, or prefer mixins with care.
